\chapter{Never, Barely, Almost, Even}
\label{ch:asi-y-incluso}
\hlchaptermodality{328}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can size a claim with asi, jamas, apenas, casi and incluso, and say which two Latin words are fused inside jamas.}

Complete ES-C328-incluso: set the manner with asi, then run the scale from jamas through apenas and casi up to incluso.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[así]{así — the word that is \emph{yes} with a run-up}

\label{lesson:ES-C328-asi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{weak}, then \emph{healthy}. (\emph{Débil}; \emph{sano}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item así que — the connector you already use. This is its first half, standing alone.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-SÍ}, two beats with the weight on the second, which is what the written accent is there to tell you. The \emph{s} is clean and hissed, never buzzed like the \emph{s} in English \emph{rose}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{así} — \textquotedblleft{}thus,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}like this,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}that way.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had \textbf{sīc}, meaning \emph{thus, in this manner}. Spanish took it twice.

Once with a small preposition glued on the front: \textbf{ad sīc}, \emph{to thus}, wore down to \textbf{así}. That is the word here — the one that points at a manner and says \emph{that one, that way}.

And once bare. \textbf{Sīc} all by itself became Spanish \textbf{sí}, \emph{yes}. A Roman answering a question affirmatively said \emph{thus} — \emph{that is how it is} — and after enough centuries of saying it, \emph{thus} stopped meaning \emph{thus} and started meaning \emph{yes}. So every \emph{sí} you have said is a worn-down \emph{so it is}, and \textbf{así es} is the full sentence it came from: \emph{that is how it is}.

English never made that leap, but it did keep the Latin word raw. When a writer quotes a mistake and puts \textbf{{[}sic{]}} after it, they are writing \emph{thus} — \emph{this is how it stood, and the error is not mine}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for saying \emph{how much} and \emph{how}. This one sets the manner; the next four set the amount.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{así}
  \item \emph{así es}
  \item \emph{así que no}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{sīc} mean? (Thus, in this manner.) And which one-letter Spanish word is \emph{sīc} with nothing added? (\emph{Sí} — yes.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jamás]{jamás — two Latin words that add up to \emph{never}}

\label{lesson:ES-C328-jamas}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{healthy}, then \emph{like this}. (\emph{Sano}; \emph{así}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mas — the second half of this word, which you already have on its own.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ja-MÁS}, the weight on the second beat. The \emph{j} is the raspy sound made at the back of the throat, nothing like an English \emph{j}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jamás} — \textquotedblleft{}never,\textquotedblright{} and in some sentences \textquotedblleft{}ever.\textquotedblright{}

Two Latin words are fused in here, and Spanish has kept both of them alive separately, so you can watch the seam.

\textbf{Iam} meant \emph{already, by now}. \textbf{Magis} meant \emph{more}. Put them together — \textbf{iam magis}, \emph{already more} — and you have a phrase about time stretching onward: \emph{ever after this}, \emph{at any point from here}.

You have met the second half. Latin \emph{magis} is the ancestor of Spanish \textbf{más}, and of the older \textbf{mas}. So \emph{jamás} is, letter by letter, \emph{already-more}.

Now the twist that makes it useful. \emph{Iam magis} originally meant \textbf{ever}, not \emph{never}. It turned negative by keeping the company of negatives: it was used so often after \emph{no} that the \emph{no} became optional and the negative meaning stuck to the word itself. French did exactly the same thing with the same two Latin words, and got \textbf{jamais}.

Both meanings survive in Spanish. After a negative it is \emph{never}: \textbf{no lo hace jamás}. On its own in a question it can still be the old \emph{ever}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five. You have the manner word and the floor of the scale — the point where an amount is nothing at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jamás}
  \item \emph{no, jamás}
  \item \emph{jamás así}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two Latin words are fused into \emph{jamás}? (\emph{Iam} and \emph{magis} — already more.) And which Spanish word is that second half on its own? (\emph{Más}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[apenas]{apenas — \emph{barely}, and the pain that is hiding in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C328-apenas}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{like this}, then \emph{never}. (\emph{Así}; \emph{jamás}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la pena — the noun sitting inside this word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-PE-nas}, three beats with the weight in the middle. No written accent, because a word ending in \emph{-s} takes its stress on the second-to-last beat by default. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{apenas} — \textquotedblleft{}barely,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}hardly,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}scarcely.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart and you find a word you already own. \textbf{A} + \textbf{penas} — \emph{at pains}, \emph{with difficulty}. To do something \emph{apenas} is to do it only by paying for it.

Latin \textbf{poena} was a \emph{penalty}, the price exacted for a wrong. Greek \textbf{poinē} before it meant a blood-price. The word travelled into every corner of English and kept its bill attached: a \textbf{penalty} is a poena, \textbf{penal} law is the law of poenas, a \textbf{penitent} pays one willingly, and a \textbf{subpoena} is a court order that names the fine you incur \emph{under} it — \emph{sub poena}, \textquotedblleft{}under penalty.\textquotedblright{}

English \textbf{pain} is the same word too, worn down through French. What started as a fine ended as the feeling of one.

Spanish kept the noun straight — \textbf{la pena}, the trouble or the sorrow — and then built this adverb on top of it. So \emph{apenas} is not a vague \emph{hardly}. It says the thing happened, and that it cost something to happen.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five. \emph{Jamás} is none of it at all; \emph{apenas} is the first sliver above none.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{apenas}
  \item \emph{apenas un poco}
  \item \emph{apenas así}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{poena} mean? (A penalty, a price paid.) And what does \emph{sub poena} mean word for word? (Under penalty.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[casi]{casi — a Latin word English borrowed without changing a letter}

\label{lesson:ES-C328-casi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{never}, then \emph{barely}. (\emph{Jamás}; \emph{apenas}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nada — the word this one likes to stand in front of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CA-si}, two even beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{s} stays crisp. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{casi} — \textquotedblleft{}almost,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}nearly.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{quasi} meant \emph{as if}, built from \textbf{quam} (\emph{as}) and \textbf{sī} (\emph{if}). It was the word a Roman reached for when a thing resembled another without being it.

Spanish wore the \emph{qu-} down to a \emph{c-} and shortened the vowel, and \textbf{quasi} became \textbf{casi}. The meaning barely moved: \emph{as if} and \emph{almost} are the same thought from two angles.

Here is the part worth noticing. English did not inherit this word — it \textbf{borrowed} it, spelling and all, and never dressed it up. A \textbf{quasi-}official statement is one that is \emph{as if} official. A \textbf{quasi-}legal arrangement is nearly but not actually legal. English speakers hyphenate a raw Latin word onto the front of nouns every day.

So \emph{casi} and \emph{quasi-} are the same five letters rearranged by time. Spanish kept it as an everyday adverb; English kept it as a formal prefix and left it looking Roman.

Pair it with what you already have: \textbf{casi nada} is \emph{almost nothing}, and it is a very common way to say \emph{hardly any}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of five. The scale now runs \emph{jamás}, \emph{apenas}, \emph{casi} — none, a sliver, nearly all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{casi}
  \item \emph{casi nada}
  \item \emph{casi todo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{quasi} mean? (As if.) And how does English still use that exact word? (As the prefix \emph{quasi-}, on anything nearly a thing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[incluso]{incluso — \emph{even}, and the door that shuts inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C328-incluso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{barely}, then \emph{almost}. (\emph{Apenas}; \emph{casi}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item todo — the word this one quietly stretches.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{in-CLU-so}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{c} before \emph{l} is a hard \emph{k}, and the two letters run together with no vowel between them. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{incluso} — \textquotedblleft{}even,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}including.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{claudere} meant \emph{to shut}. Put \textbf{in-} on the front and you get \textbf{inclūdere}, \emph{to shut in}, whose past participle is \textbf{inclūsus} — \emph{shut inside}. Spanish took that participle whole.

That is the whole idea of the word. When you say \emph{incluso}, you are naming something and shutting it inside the group, especially when the listener would have expected it left out. \emph{Even that one is in here.}

The Latin door swings in every direction in English, and you can hear the same four letters each time. To \textbf{include} is to shut in. To \textbf{enclose} is to shut around. To \textbf{exclude} is to shut out. To \textbf{seclude} is to shut apart. A \textbf{recluse} has shut himself away. To \textbf{conclude} is to shut a matter completely, which is why a \textbf{conclusion} ends things. And plain \textbf{close} is the same verb, worn smooth by French.

So a word that now means \emph{even} is, underneath, a door being pulled shut with one more thing on the inside.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for how much: \emph{jamás}, \emph{apenas}, \emph{casi}, \emph{incluso}, and \emph{así} for how. Between them you can size almost any claim somebody makes to you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{incluso}
  \item \emph{incluso hoy}
  \item \emph{incluso así}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{claudere} mean? (To shut.) And what is a \textbf{recluse}, taken literally? (Somebody shut away.)
\end{tcolorbox}
